title: First Aid
description: What to do, and in what order, in the first minutes of an emergency: scene safety, the primary survey, CPR and AED, choking, bleeding, burns, fractures, head injury, heart attack, stroke, allergic reactions, poisoning and heat or cold. This course teaches the knowledge; it does not replace hands-on training with a certified instructor.
audience: A capable adult with no medical training who wants to know what a first aider does and why, before or alongside a hands-on course. They need only everyday knowledge of the body. Nothing here qualifies the learner to give first aid in a workplace or to hold a certificate.
outcomes: You'll be able to make a scene safe, call for help with the information a dispatcher needs, and carry out a primary survey in the right order.
You'll be able to state the adult CPR figures (where to press, how fast, how deep, and the compression-to-breath ratio) and the steps for using an AED.
You'll be able to tell mild from severe choking and give the right sequence for each.
You'll be able to control severe bleeding, treat a burn, and support a suspected fracture or head injury without making it worse.
You'll be able to recognise a heart attack, a stroke, anaphylaxis, poisoning, heat stroke and hypothermia, and say what to do and what to avoid.

modules.title: First steps at any emergency
modules.summary: The role and limits of a first aider, scene safety, calling for help, the primary survey and the recovery position.

modules.title: Resuscitation and choking
modules.summary: Adult CPR, the AED, children and infants, and choking.

modules.title: Injuries
modules.summary: Bleeding and shock, burns, fractures, and head and spine injury.

modules.title: Sudden illness and the environment
modules.summary: Heart attack, stroke, allergic reactions, poisoning, heat, cold and bites.

lessons.title: What a first aider does, and where it stops
lessons.objective: Describe the aims of first aid, make a scene safe, and give an emergency call the information a dispatcher needs.

concepts.title: Aims of first aid
concepts.summary: To preserve life, to prevent the condition worsening and to promote recovery, until professional help takes over.

concepts.title: Scene safety
concepts.summary: A first aider checks for danger to themselves, the casualty and bystanders before approaching, because a second casualty helps no one.

concepts.title: Calling for help
concepts.summary: The call to the local emergency number gives the exact location, what happened, how many people are hurt and their state, and the dispatcher's instructions are followed.

concepts.title: Limits of this course
concepts.summary: Reading a guideline is not training; hands-on practice with a certified instructor is how skills like CPR are learned and kept.

misconceptions: Learners rush to the casualty; a first aider who becomes a casualty cannot help, so danger comes first.
Learners think hanging up quickly saves time; the dispatcher can give instructions, such as CPR coaching, and needs the address confirmed.
Learners think they can be sued for helping; legal protection varies by country and the course must say it does not give legal advice.
sequence: Begin from a concrete scene: a person lying on a road. Ask what the first aider checks before touching them.
State the aims of first aid and how they differ from medical treatment.
Scene safety: traffic, fire, fumes, electricity, unstable structures, violence. Make safe or stay away and call.
The emergency call: location, what happened, number of casualties, their state, what has been done; stay on the line; send someone to meet the ambulance.
Consent: a conscious adult agrees to help; an unresponsive person's consent is implied.

State plainly that the course is knowledge only and does not replace a hands-on course. Give the local emergency number as a setting for the learner to look up; numbers differ by country (for example 112, 999, 911, 000).
examples: A person lies beside a car on a busy road. The first aider switches on hazard lights, looks for traffic before stepping out, and calls the emergency number before approaching.
A dispatcher script: 'I am at 14 Mill Road, outside the library. A man of about 60 collapsed and is not responding. He is not breathing normally. I am starting CPR.'

figures.shows: A road scene drawn from above with hazards marked (traffic, spilled fuel, downed cable) and a casualty. Switchable views show the safe approach path.
figures.learnerAction: Tap each hazard and drag the first aider to a safe position.

figures.shows: Five cards for an emergency call, shuffled.

questionPlan.sample: You arrive at a collapse beside a fallen electrical cable. What do you do first?
choices: Pull the person away by the arms
Keep away from the cable and call the emergency number
Touch the cable with a stick
questionPlan.answer: Keep away from the cable and call the emergency number

questionPlan.sample: During the call, when do you end it?
choices: As soon as you say the address
When the dispatcher tells you to
questionPlan.answer: When the dispatcher tells you to

questionPlan.sample: Recall: why does this course not replace a certified hands-on course?
questionPlan.answer: Skills such as CPR and AED use are learned and checked by practice with an instructor and a manikin, which reading cannot give.

lessons.title: The primary survey
lessons.objective: Carry out a primary survey in order: response, airway, breathing and circulation, and decide whether the casualty needs CPR.

concepts.title: Primary survey
concepts.summary: A quick ordered check for life-threatening problems: danger, response, airway, breathing, severe bleeding.

concepts.title: Response check
concepts.summary: Speak loudly, tap the shoulders; no response means the person is unresponsive.

concepts.title: Normal breathing
concepts.summary: Look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds; occasional gasps are not normal breathing.

concepts.title: Opening the airway
concepts.summary: Tilting the head back and lifting the chin lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat.

misconceptions: Learners treat noisy gasping as breathing; these gasps (agonal breathing) occur in the first minutes of cardiac arrest and mean CPR is needed.
Learners spend a long time checking a pulse; lay rescuers check breathing, not pulse.
sequence: Danger already checked; now response.
Unresponsive: shout for help, call or send someone to call.
Open the airway with head tilt and chin lift.
Check breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
Not breathing normally: begin CPR (next module). Breathing normally: recovery position (next lesson).
Look for life-threatening bleeding at any point.
examples: A man on a pavement does not answer when spoken to or tapped. The first aider tilts his head back, looks for chest movement and listens for 10 seconds, hearing only occasional snoring gasps. This is not normal breathing.

figures.shows: Cards for the primary survey steps.
A flow chart: response? breathing normally? with two outcomes.
figures.learnerAction: Follow a case through the flow chart.

questionPlan.sample: Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than how many seconds?
An unresponsive adult makes occasional gasping sounds, once every few seconds. Is this normal breathing?
Which comes first after confirming the scene is safe?

lessons.title: Unresponsive and breathing: the recovery position
lessons.objective: Decide when to use the recovery position and describe how it protects the airway.

concepts.title: Recovery position
concepts.summary: Lying on the side with the head tilted back and the mouth angled down so that fluid drains and the tongue cannot block the airway.

concepts.title: When to use it
concepts.summary: For an unresponsive person who is breathing normally and has no suspected injury that forbids moving them.

misconceptions: Learners put anyone who is unwell in the recovery position; it is for people who are unresponsive, breathing normally and need their airway protected.
Learners leave the person unwatched; breathing can stop, so keep checking and be ready to start CPR.
sequence: Why an unresponsive person on their back is at risk: the tongue falls back and vomit can be inhaled.
Steps in plain words: arm placement, bent knee, roll to the side, tilt head back.
Keep checking breathing and call for help.
When not to move: suspected spine injury and the airway cannot be kept open (airway takes priority).
Pregnancy: lie on the left side (verify against IFRC).
examples: A person found after a faint who stays unresponsive for several minutes but breathes normally is placed in the recovery position while the ambulance is called.

figures.shows: Four step diagrams of rolling a person into the recovery position, switchable by step.
figures.learnerAction: Step through and name the position of the top arm and knee.

questionPlan.sample: An unresponsive person is breathing normally and has no known injury. What is the next step after calling for help?
After placing someone in the recovery position, you should:
The recovery position puts the person on their ___.

lessons.title: CPR for an adult
lessons.objective: State the adult CPR figures (place, rate, depth, recoil, ratio) and work out how long a cycle takes.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest
concepts.summary: The heart stops pumping effectively, so the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

concepts.title: Chest compressions
concepts.summary: Pressing on the centre of the chest 100 to 120 times a minute, 5 to 6 cm deep, allowing the chest to recoil fully each time.

concepts.title: Compression-to-breath ratio
concepts.summary: A trained rescuer gives 30 compressions then 2 breaths; an untrained rescuer, or one unwilling to give breaths, gives compressions alone.

concepts.title: Minimising interruptions
concepts.summary: Blood flow to the brain stops when compressions stop, so pauses are kept as short as possible.

misconceptions: Learners press gently for fear of breaking ribs; ribs can break, and too shallow compressions do not circulate blood.
Learners lean on the chest between compressions; incomplete recoil stops the heart refilling.
Learners wait for certainty before starting; if unresponsive and not breathing normally, start.
sequence: Why the first minutes matter: the heart's rhythm and the brain's oxygen.
Hand position: heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over hands.
Rate, depth, full recoil.
Give 30 compressions then 2 breaths if trained; hands-only if not.
A compression cycle of 30 at 100 per minute lasts 18 s; at 120 per minute, 15 s.
Continue until help takes over, the person shows signs of life or you are too exhausted; swap rescuers every 2 minutes if possible.
Say clearly that this describes the guideline and that only practice on a manikin with an instructor teaches the correct force and rhythm.
examples: 30 compressions at 100 per minute take 30 / 100 × 60 = 18 s; at 120 per minute they take 30 / 120 × 60 = 15 s.
Two minutes of compressions at 110 per minute without interruption are 220 compressions.

figures.shows: Side view of a kneeling rescuer with arms straight over the centre of the chest, and a marked 5 to 6 cm depth scale on the chest.
A beat track at 100, 110 and 120 per minute as three lines of ticks over 10 seconds (the answer to the cycle-time question is not shown).
figures.learnerAction: Count beats in 10 seconds for each rate.

questionPlan.sample: What is the upper limit of the adult CPR compression rate, in compressions per minute?
What is the minimum compression depth for an adult, in cm?
At 120 compressions per minute, how many seconds do 30 compressions take?
A trained rescuer gives 30 compressions to how many breaths? (as a ratio 30:?)

historyNotes: Guideline bodies review resuscitation science on a cycle; the IFRC guidelines are issued in editions (2016, 2020 and 2025 are the editions referred to in IFRC material), and the writer must state which edition the lesson follows.

lessons.title: Using an AED
lessons.objective: List the steps for using an automated external defibrillator and say what a shock does and does not do.

concepts.title: Automated external defibrillator
concepts.summary: A device that analyses the heart's rhythm and, if it finds a shockable rhythm, tells the rescuer to deliver a shock.

concepts.title: Shockable rhythm
concepts.summary: A chaotic or very fast rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) that a shock can stop so the heart may restart normally.

concepts.title: Pad placement
concepts.summary: Two adhesive pads go on bare, dry skin in the positions shown on the pads.

misconceptions: Learners think an AED restarts a stopped heart ('flatline'); it treats only certain rhythms, and CPR continues when no shock is advised.
Learners fear harming the casualty; the device decides and will not shock if it is not needed.
Learners stop CPR to wait for the AED; CPR continues until the AED is ready to analyse.
sequence: Send someone to fetch the AED when the call is made.
Switch on and follow the spoken prompts.
Bare the chest, dry it, attach pads as pictured.
Stand clear during analysis and shock.
Resume CPR immediately after the shock, or if no shock is advised.
Continue to follow prompts; the AED re-analyses about every 2 minutes.
examples: A rescuer is doing compressions when a bystander arrives with an AED. The second person attaches the pads while compressions continue; compressions pause only when the AED says it is analysing.

figures.shows: A torso with two pad positions marked and a blank panel for the AED prompts, switchable to the prompt sequence.
figures.learnerAction: Place the pads by dragging them.

figures.shows: Seven AED step cards.

questionPlan.sample: What do you do straight after an AED delivers a shock?
choices: Check the pulse for a minute
Wait for the ambulance without touching

questionPlan.sample: While the AED analyses the rhythm, who may touch the casualty?
About how many minutes of CPR pass between AED rhythm analyses?

lessons.title: Resuscitation for children and infants
lessons.objective: State how resuscitation differs for children and infants and why, following the guideline edition cited.

concepts.title: Different causes
concepts.summary: Children and infants more often stop breathing first, because of choking, drowning or illness, so breaths matter more.

concepts.title: Scaled compressions
concepts.summary: Compress the chest by about one third of its depth, at the same rate as for an adult.

concepts.title: Infant technique
concepts.summary: The rescuer uses the technique the cited guideline gives for infants (two thumbs encircling the chest or two fingers; writer must confirm the technique and the child ratio for the edition used).

misconceptions: Learners apply adult depth to a child; excessive force injures, so depth is scaled to the chest.
Learners skip breaths for children; for children and infants, breaths are an important part of resuscitation.
sequence: Why the cause differs.
Same rate; depth about one third of the chest.
Opening the airway: neutral head for infants.
Starting with breaths where the guideline says so.
Hand or finger placement by age.
Compare with the adult figures in a table.
examples: Worked example to be written from the guideline's own stated depths for children and infants once confirmed; do not invent centimetre figures.

figures.shows: Adult, child and infant side by side: hand position, depth, rate, ratio. Cells for ratio and technique filled only from the confirmed edition.

questionPlan.sample: For a child, compression depth is about what fraction of the chest depth?
Is the compression rate for a child different from an adult's 100 to 120 per minute?
Recall: why are breaths more important for children than for adults?
questionPlan.answer: Children more often stop breathing first from choking, drowning or illness, so low oxygen is the usual cause.

lessons.title: Choking
lessons.objective: Tell mild from severe choking and give the right sequence for adults and infants.

concepts.title: Mild choking
concepts.summary: The person can speak, cough and breathe; encourage them to keep coughing.

concepts.title: Severe choking
concepts.summary: The person cannot speak, cough effectively or breathe, may clutch the throat and goes silent.

concepts.title: Back blows and thrusts
concepts.summary: For an adult with severe choking give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, and alternate; for an infant use back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.

misconceptions: Learners slap the back of someone who is coughing well; a good cough is the best treatment, and a blow may move the object deeper.
Learners use abdominal thrusts on infants; infants get back blows and chest thrusts.
Learners reach into the mouth blindly; look, and remove an object only if you can see it.
sequence: Ask the person: 'Are you choking?' If they can answer, it is mild.
Mild: encourage coughing and stay with them.
Severe adult: lean the person forward; 5 back blows with the heel of the hand; if that fails, 5 abdominal thrusts; alternate; call the emergency number.
Infant: face down along the forearm, 5 back blows, then face up, 5 chest thrusts.
Unresponsive: start CPR.
Anyone who received abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor.
examples: A man at a table stops talking, clutches his throat and cannot cough. He is severely choking; the first aider leans him forward and gives 5 back blows.

figures.shows: A decision chart: can they cough or speak? with two branches, and for the severe branch the back-blow and thrust steps drawn.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the branch for four cases.

questionPlan.sample: A person coughs strongly and can say 'I'm choking'. This is:
In severe choking in an adult, how many back blows do you give before switching to abdominal thrusts?
What is given to a choking infant after back blows?

lessons.title: Severe bleeding and shock
lessons.objective: Control severe external bleeding with direct pressure, know when a tourniquet is used, and recognise shock.

concepts.title: Direct pressure
concepts.summary: Firm, continuous pressure on the wound with a pad or the hands, kept on until help arrives.

concepts.title: Tourniquet
concepts.summary: A band tightened above a bleeding limb wound when direct pressure cannot control life-threatening bleeding; the time is noted and it is not loosened.

concepts.title: Shock
concepts.summary: Failure of circulation to deliver enough blood to the body, shown by pale, cold, clammy skin, fast breathing and pulse, weakness and confusion.

misconceptions: Learners lift the dressing to check; lifting disturbs the clot, so add more dressings on top.
Learners reach for a tourniquet first; direct pressure is first-line, and the tourniquet is for pressure that fails or limb injuries that cannot be pressed.
Learners give a drink to someone in shock; they may need surgery, so give nothing by mouth.
sequence: Gloves or a barrier if available; wash hands afterwards.
Press directly on the wound; add dressings if blood soaks through.
Bandage firmly over the pad.
When pressure fails: tourniquet on the limb above the wound, note the time.
Shock signs; lay the person down, keep warm, call the emergency number, give nothing to eat or drink.
Special cases: a nosebleed (lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose; writer to cite the time from the guideline).
examples: A cut forearm is soaking a pad. The first aider presses on the pad, places a second pad on top without removing the first, and bandages firmly.

figures.shows: A forearm wound with a pad and bandage, and a switchable second view showing a tourniquet above the wound with a time tag.
Signs of early and late shock.

questionPlan.sample: Blood soaks through the pad you are pressing on. What do you do?
choices: Remove it and apply a fresh pad
Add another pad on top and keep pressing
questionPlan.answer: Add another pad on top and keep pressing

questionPlan.sample: A band tightened above a limb wound when direct pressure fails is a ___.
Which set of signs suggests shock?
choices: Pale, cold, clammy, with fast breathing
Red and sweaty with slow pulse
questionPlan.answer: Pale, cold, clammy, with fast breathing

lessons.title: Burns and scalds
lessons.objective: Treat a thermal burn with cooling, dress it correctly, and decide when a burn needs urgent care; treat chemical and electrical burns safely.

concepts.title: Cooling
concepts.summary: Cool a thermal burn promptly with cool running water for the time the guideline gives, to reduce damage and pain.

concepts.title: Dressing
concepts.summary: Cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-fluffy, non-sticking dressing or cling film applied lengthways.

concepts.title: Burns needing urgent help
concepts.summary: Burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, in infants, or caused by chemicals or electricity need urgent medical care.

misconceptions: Learners apply ice, butter or toothpaste; ice can add cold injury and greasy substances trap heat and need cleaning off.
Learners burst blisters; intact blisters protect the wound.
Learners pull off clothing stuck to the burn; stuck material is left and the area cooled.
sequence: Stop the burning: remove from the source, put out flames (stop, drop, roll), switch off electricity before approaching.
Cool with cool running water for the time given by the guideline (writer to confirm the number of minutes from IFRC; some other bodies give longer).
Remove rings and watches near the burn, before swelling, unless stuck.
Cover loosely.
Chemical burns: remove contaminated clothing and flush with plenty of running water; call for help.
Electrical burns: ensure power is off; always seek medical care.
examples: A child pulls a cup of hot tea onto their arm. The first aider removes the wet clothing that is not stuck, holds the arm under cool running water, then covers it loosely with cling film.

figures.shows: Four sketched actions after a burn (ice, running water, butter, bandage tightly).
Burn types (thermal, chemical, electrical) and their first actions.

questionPlan.sample: Which should you not do to a thermal burn?
Which cooling method is recommended for a thermal burn?
A chemical splashes on a person's arm. After making the scene safe, what is the main treatment?
choices: Flush the area with plenty of running water
questionPlan.answer: Flush the area with plenty of running water

lessons.title: Fractures, sprains and dislocations
lessons.objective: Support a suspected fracture in the position found, recognise signs that need urgent care, and avoid moving the injured part.

concepts.title: Fracture
concepts.summary: A broken bone; signs include pain, swelling, deformity, bruising and inability to use the part.

concepts.title: Immobilising
concepts.summary: Supporting the injured part in the position found, using padding, a sling or a splint, to reduce pain and further damage.

concepts.title: Open fracture
concepts.summary: A fracture with a wound where the bone may show; control bleeding and cover the wound without pressing on the bone.

misconceptions: Learners try to straighten a deformed limb; moving it can damage vessels and nerves.
Learners test the injured part by asking the person to move it; movement causes harm and pain.
sequence: Recognise signs; do not test by movement.
Support in the position found; pad around it.
A sling for an arm; a splint only if trained and help is far.
Cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling and pain.
Check feeling, colour and warmth beyond the injury, repeatedly.
Urgent: deformity with poor circulation, open fracture, suspected hip, spine or pelvis injury.
examples: A fall on an outstretched hand leaves a swollen, deformed wrist. The first aider supports it in the position found with a sling, applies a wrapped cold pack and calls for help.

figures.shows: Arm in a triangular sling, with switchable layers for padding and cold pack.

questionPlan.sample: A deformed forearm is suspected broken. You:
choices: Support it in the position found
Ask the person to move the fingers repeatedly
questionPlan.answer: Support it in the position found

questionPlan.sample: Which injury needs urgent help?
choices: Bruise on a shin with full movement

questionPlan.sample: Keeping an injured part from moving is called ___ it.

lessons.title: Head and spine injury
lessons.objective: Recognise a concussion and the warning signs that need urgent care, and say when to keep a person still.

concepts.title: Concussion
concepts.summary: A temporary disturbance of brain function after a blow, with headache, confusion, memory loss or dizziness.

concepts.title: Red flags
concepts.summary: Loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, drowsiness, seizure, weakness or clear fluid from the nose or ears mean urgent medical care.

concepts.title: Spinal precautions
concepts.summary: With a suspected spine injury, keep the head and body still unless the person is in danger or cannot keep an open airway.

misconceptions: Learners think a person must be knocked out to have a serious head injury; many are not.
Learners think a person with concussion must be kept awake all night; the key is to watch for worsening and seek care, and the writer follows the guideline wording.
sequence: Mechanism: a fall from height or a high-speed crash raises suspicion of a spine injury.
Concussion signs and rest.
Red flags that call for an ambulance.
Spine: hold the head still in the position found; do not move unless there is danger.
Airway comes first: if the person is unresponsive and cannot be kept open, move them as carefully as possible.
Helmets: leave on unless they block the airway or breathing (writer to confirm with the guideline).
examples: A cyclist falls and is briefly confused but walks. Twenty minutes later she vomits twice and becomes drowsy: a red flag, call the emergency number.

figures.shows: Signs at the time of injury and signs that appear later.
figures.learnerAction: Sort sample signs into 'watch' or 'call now'.

questionPlan.sample: After a head injury, which sign needs urgent care?
A fall from a ladder with neck pain. The person is awake and breathing. You:
choices: Keep the head and body still and call for help
questionPlan.answer: Keep the head and body still and call for help

questionPlan.sample: Recall: when does the airway take priority over keeping the spine still?
questionPlan.answer: When an unresponsive person cannot keep an open airway; maintaining breathing outweighs the spinal risk.

lessons.title: Heart attack and stroke
lessons.objective: Tell the signs of a heart attack and a stroke, and give the first aid for each, including what to avoid.

concepts.title: Heart attack
concepts.summary: A blocked coronary artery starves heart muscle of blood, causing chest pain or pressure that may spread to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating and breathlessness.

concepts.title: Stroke
concepts.summary: An interruption of blood to part of the brain, from a blockage or a bleed.

concepts.title: FAST
concepts.summary: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call the emergency number.

misconceptions: Learners wait to see if stroke symptoms pass; time lost loses brain tissue, so call at once.
Learners give aspirin to a stroke patient; some strokes are bleeds, and aspirin can make them worse.
Learners expect crushing chest pain only; women and older people may have breathlessness, nausea or back or jaw pain.
sequence: Heart attack signs.
First aid: call the emergency number, rest in a comfortable position (often half-sitting), loosen tight clothing, stay with the person.
Aspirin: for an adult with suspected heart attack, one dose chewed if not allergic and not told to avoid it; writer must confirm the dose and conditions in the IFRC text.
If the person becomes unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED.
Stroke: FAST test, note the time symptoms began, call at once, give nothing to eat or drink, no aspirin.
examples: A man in his 60s feels pressure in his chest and pain spreading to his left arm, with cold sweat. The first aider calls for help and helps him sit, half-reclined, supported.

figures.shows: Four panels for FAST, each showing the sign (a drooping smile, an arm drifting down, slurred speech bubble, a clock).
figures.learnerAction: Identify the sign in each of three cases.

questionPlan.sample: In FAST, the T stands for ___.
A person suddenly has slurred speech and a drooping face. What do you do?
choices: Call the emergency number at once
questionPlan.answer: Call the emergency number at once

questionPlan.sample: A person with suspected heart attack is breathing and awake. Which position is usually best?

lessons.title: Allergic reactions and poisoning
lessons.objective: Recognise anaphylaxis and use an adrenaline auto-injector, and respond to poisoning without making it worse.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis
concepts.summary: A severe, rapid allergic reaction that can narrow the airway and drop blood pressure.

concepts.title: Adrenaline auto-injector
concepts.summary: A pen that injects adrenaline into the outer thigh, through clothing if needed, held in place for the time on its instructions.

concepts.title: Poison information
concepts.summary: A poison centre or emergency service gives advice that depends on the substance, the amount and the time.

misconceptions: Learners wait for the reaction to ease before using the injector; give it early, since delay is dangerous.
Learners make a poisoned person vomit; this can burn the throat again or send material into the lungs.
Learners think an auto-injector can harm a person with no reaction; it is the safer error.
sequence: Signs: swelling of lips or face, hives, difficulty breathing, wheeze, faintness.
Call the emergency number, use the person's own auto-injector in the outer thigh.
Position: lying with legs raised, or sitting if breathing is hard; do not let them stand.
A second dose may be given after a stated interval if no improvement; writer to confirm the interval from the guideline.
Poisoning: make the scene safe (fumes, carbon monoxide), call the emergency number or poison centre, find the container, do not induce vomiting, give nothing to drink unless advised.
Skin and eye contact: remove contaminated clothing and rinse with running water.
examples: A child with a known nut allergy eats a biscuit; within minutes her lips swell and she wheezes. A teacher calls for help and gives her auto-injector into the outer thigh through her leggings.

figures.shows: An outer thigh with the injection zone marked, and a pen with its parts labelled.

questionPlan.sample: Where is an adrenaline auto-injector given?
Someone has swallowed a household cleaner. You should:
choices: Call the emergency number or poison centre and keep the container
questionPlan.answer: Call the emergency number or poison centre and keep the container

questionPlan.sample: Which combination suggests anaphylaxis?
choices: Swollen lips with wheezing after a sting
questionPlan.answer: Swollen lips with wheezing after a sting

lessons.title: Heat, cold and bites
lessons.objective: Recognise heat exhaustion, heat stroke and hypothermia, and give first aid; know what to do for snake bite and stings.

concepts.title: Heat exhaustion
concepts.summary: Heavy sweating, weakness and headache in the heat; treated by moving to a cool place, resting and drinking fluids.

concepts.title: Heat stroke
concepts.summary: A medical emergency with very high body temperature and confusion or collapse; cool the person quickly and call the emergency number.

concepts.title: Hypothermia
concepts.summary: A body temperature low enough to impair function, with shivering, confusion and drowsiness; prevent further heat loss and handle gently.

misconceptions: Learners treat heat stroke as exhaustion and give fluids; confusion means an emergency and rapid cooling is the priority.
Learners rub a frostbitten area or a cold person's limbs; rubbing damages tissue and rough handling can upset the heart.
Learners cut or suck a snake bite; neither helps.
sequence: Heat exhaustion: cool place, remove excess clothing, sips of fluid.
Heat stroke: confusion or collapse with hot skin; call, cool the person quickly (cold water immersion if possible, or wet skin and fan).
Hypothermia: shelter, remove wet clothing, insulate from the ground, cover head, warm sweet drink if alert, handle gently; call for help.
Frostbite: protect the area, do not rub, rewarm only if refreezing cannot happen.

Bites and stings: remove a sting, cool the area, watch for anaphylaxis; snake bite: keep calm and still and get help; writer to follow the guideline about pressure immobilisation, which depends on the snake species in the country.
examples: A runner on a hot day stumbles, is confused and has hot, dry skin. This is heat stroke: the first aider calls for help and cools him with water and fanning.

figures.shows: Heat exhaustion beside heat stroke: signs and first aid, with hidden answers for a sorting task.
figures.learnerAction: Sort signs into the two columns.

questionPlan.sample: A hot, confused person who has collapsed after exercise needs:
choices: Rapid cooling and the emergency number
questionPlan.answer: Rapid cooling and the emergency number

questionPlan.sample: A cold, shivering, drowsy person should be:
choices: Handled gently and insulated from the cold
questionPlan.answer: Handled gently and insulated from the cold

questionPlan.sample: Which should you not do for a snake bite?
choices: Keep the person calm and still
Cut the wound and suck out the venom
questionPlan.answer: Cut the wound and suck out the venom

courseCheck: A mixed check, all markable without free text: order the scene and primary survey; decide whether breathing is normal; state the adult CPR rate limits, depth and ratio and compute a cycle time; order AED steps; classify choking and give the sequence; control bleeding; pick the first action for a burn; support a fracture; spot red flags after a head injury; recognise FAST and heart attack; use an auto-injector site; separate heat stroke from exhaustion. Include a statement that the course is not a substitute for certified hands-on training and that learners should find a local accredited course.
platformNeeds: A persistent short notice on every first-aid lesson stating it does not replace certified hands-on training (one line, shown once per lesson, not a repeated banner).
A tap-tempo or metronome figure at 100 to 120 per minute, where the learner taps and sees their rate and whether it lies in range. Fallback: data_series beat tracks.
A setting for the learner's country, so the emergency number and any national variation (for example 112, 999, 911, 000) can be shown correctly.
A guideline-edition tag on the course and per lesson (for example 'IFRC 2025'), shown where a number is given, and a flag to hold the course for review when the edition changes.
An annotated body-diagram figure with tap targets (pad positions, injection site, pressure points) without revealing answers; the fallback is svg_figure.
A branching scenario figure where the learner picks the next action and sees a consequence, for the primary survey and choking decisions.
unverified: No source could be opened in this session (the network blocked ifrc.org, redcross.org, redcross.org.uk, erc.edu and every other host), so every source has verified: false, and no figure below was checked against the IFRC text. Before any lesson is written, the writer must open the IFRC 2025 guidelines and confirm each figure, and the licence terms for reuse. Recorded licence for the IFRC guidelines: not confirmed; treat as all rights reserved; paraphrase only.

Corroborated only by a web-search summary of Resuscitation Council UK and ERC 2025 material (not IFRC): adult compressions 100 to 120 per minute, depth 5 to 6 cm, 30:2 ratio, and avoiding depth above 6 cm. IFRC 2025 agreement is assumed, not seen.

From memory of the IFRC 2020 guidelines and common national guidance, not rechecked: look for breathing for no more than 10 seconds; AED re-analysis about every 2 minutes; 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts for adult severe choking, and back blows then chest thrusts for infants; direct pressure first and a tourniquet when pressure fails; cooling a burn with running water; do not straighten a fracture; FAST for stroke; adrenaline auto-injector in the outer thigh; do not induce vomiting.

Left deliberately open for the writer to fill from the confirmed IFRC text: the number of minutes to cool a burn (some bodies say 10, others 20); the aspirin dose and conditions for heart attack; the interval before a second adrenaline dose; the child and infant CPR ratio, whether to start with rescue breaths, and the infant compression technique (two-thumb encircling versus two fingers), which changed in some 2025 national guidance; nosebleed pressure time; the helmet advice; pregnancy positioning in the recovery position; pressure immobilisation for snake bite.
Whether the IFRC 2025 edition keeps the same recovery-position, shock-positioning and leg-raising advice as the 2020 edition was not checked.

The statement that IFRC editions exist for 2016, 2020 and 2025 is from memory and from a search summary that said the 2025 edition replaces the 2016 guidelines; the 2020 edition's existence should be confirmed.
Local emergency numbers (112, 999, 911, 000) are given as examples and are from memory.
